# Printervention: A Journey to Save Old Printers

In an era where digital photos reign supreme, the charm of holding a physical photograph in your hands remains unparalleled. This sentiment sparked a personal project for one tech enthusiast who recently undertook the challenge of reviving an old Canon SELPHY photo printer. What began as a simple trade of a 3D printer for a photo printer evolved into a full-fledged mission to bridge the gap between outdated hardware and modern technology.

## A Printer with Limitations

The Canon SELPHY, while being a compact and cost-effective solution for printing photos, had its flaws. Notably, it lacks support for both Mac and Windows operating systems. Faced with this limitation, the author turned to a Manjaro Linux machine, utilizing the Common Unix Printing System (CUPS) and Gutenprint drivers to establish a print server. This setup enabled printing from both Macs and iPhones via AirPrint, making it accessible to users who might not be technically inclined.

## Embracing Nostalgia

This endeavor was not merely about functionality; it was also a journey into nostalgia. The author reminisced about the joy of printing physical photos, contrasting it with the convenience of digital images. The idea of creating a print server for family members was considered but ultimately deemed impractical due to the clutter of extra plugs and wires. Instead, the focus shifted to developing a solution that would allow non-technical users to easily print photos, potentially saving many printers from being discarded.

## The Development Journey

Initially, the author set out to create a native Mac application using Claude Code within a Linux virtual machine. However, recognizing the need for a more universal solution, the project pivoted to a web app named [printerface.app](https://printerface.app) (and its alternate domain, printervention.app). This innovative approach leverages WebUSB to allow users to print without the need for installation, all from their web browsers.

The app runs an x86 CPU emulator in the browser, executing Alpine Linux with CUPS and Gutenprint drivers. By connecting to printers over WebUSB, the app retrieves essential details such as make and model and installs the appropriate Gutenprint driver. Users can upload their files to the emulated machine and send print commands seamlessly.

## Overcoming Technical Hurdles

The path to success was not without its challenges. Early iterations faced issues with one-way data flow, leading the author to implement a two-way bridge using USB/IP and tcpip.js for improved communication. Subsequent improvements tackled various photo sizes and formats, including embedding JPEGs in PDFs and converting HEIC files for compatibility.

## Looking Ahead

The app has been successfully tested on a range of photo printers, with aspirations for broader compatibility in the future. Plans are underway to improve the app and add more printer driver packages. Interestingly, the author has expressed a preference for forming partnerships with printer consumables firms rather than open-sourcing the project, aiming for a sustainable model that benefits both users
